```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(bdhs)
```

The same DHS variable name does not always mean the same thing across BDHS
rounds:

* **Divisions** went from 5 (1993-94) to 6 (Sylhet), 7 (Rangpur, 2011) and 8
  (Mymensingh, 2017-18). When Mymensingh became code 5, Rajshahi, Rangpur and
  Sylhet each moved up one code. Spellings changed too: "barisal" and
  "chittagong" became "barishal" and "chattogram" in 2022.
* **Answer categories** change. Places of delivery, types of provider and
  water and toilet types get new codes as the questionnaires evolve, and the
  letters of the delivery-assistance variables `m3a`-`m3n` shift between
  rounds.
* **Some content lives elsewhere.** The wealth index of 1993-94, 1996-97 and
  1999-2000 is in separate WI files, and the WHO growth-standard z-scores of
  1996-97 to 2004 are in separate HW files.
* **Some value labels in the files are simply wrong**, for example religion
  in 1993-94, and roof material in 1999-2000.

`bdhs_variable()` shows the problem for any variable, using the bundled
codebooks:

```{r}
bdhs_variable("v024", recode = "KR")[, c("survey_id", "label", "value_labels", "label_drift")]
```

## The harmonized variables

bdhs ships a crosswalk with rules for `r nrow(bdhs_harmonized_vars())`
harmonized variables. Each rule names the source variables and code mapping
for every round, and was checked against the real files and against official
DHS estimates.

```{r}
hv <- bdhs_harmonized_vars()
hv[, c("name", "label", "comparability")]
table(hv$comparability)
```

`comparability` tells you how far a variable can be compared:

* `"full"`: same meaning in every round.
* `"partial"`: comparable, but with documented caveats, such as new
  categories or one round missing.
* `"break"`: definitions differ. The division as surveyed is one example,
  because the boundaries themselves changed.

`bdhs_harmonized_vars(survey)` shows the rules for one round, with the
source variables:

```{r}
r <- bdhs_harmonized_vars(2004)
r[r$name %in% c("wealth_quintile", "facility_delivery", "haz_who"), c("name", "method", "source", "available", "note")]
```

## Harmonizing a dataset

`bdhs_harmonize()` adds the harmonized columns to your data. The original
DHS columns stay as they were.

```{r}
kr <- bdhs_simulate(2017, "KR")
h <- bdhs_harmonize(kr, vars = c("division_surveyed", "division_trend6", "residence",
                                 "wealth_quintile", "facility_delivery", "csection"))
h[1:6, c("v024", "division_surveyed", "division_trend6", "residence", "facility_delivery", "csection")]
```

Without `vars`, every harmonized variable that applies to the recode is
created. Rules written for children (KR) also apply to women (IR) and births
(BR) where they concern the mother. Variables with a household equivalent
also work in the household (HR) and member (PR) files.

### Division layouts

| Variable | Layout |
|---|---|
| `division_surveyed` | Divisions as they existed at the survey (5 to 8) |
| `division_trend6` | Six divisions: Rangpur in Rajshahi, Mymensingh in Dhaka |
| `division_trend5` | Five 1993-94 divisions: Sylhet also in Chattogram |
| `division_backcast8` | 2022's eight divisions, rebuilt from districts where possible |

The bundled `bdhs_regions` table holds the same crosswalk for every survey,
with the codes as they appear in the files:

```{r}
bdhs_regions[bdhs_regions$survey_id == "BD2017DHS", c("region_code", "region_label", "division", "trend6", "trend5")]
```

## Trends with pooled, harmonized data

Pool rounds with `harmonize = TRUE`, then analyse with the pooled design:

```{r}
years <- c(2004, 2011, 2017, 2022)
rounds <- lapply(seq_along(years), function(i) bdhs_simulate(years[i], "KR", seed = i))
pooled <- bdhs_pool(rounds, harmonize = TRUE, vars = c("division_trend6", "csection"))
des <- bdhs_design(pooled)
survey::svyby(~csection, ~survey_id, des, survey::svymean, na.rm = TRUE)
```

(The values are random because the data are simulated. With real data this
is the C-section trend.)

## Early rounds: wealth and z-scores from separate files

For 1993-94 to 1999-2000 the wealth index comes from a WI file, and the WHO
z-scores for 1996-97 to 2004 come from an HW file. Merge them first, and
`bdhs_harmonize()` picks them up:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
kr <- bdhs_read(2004, "KR")
hw <- bdhs_read(2004, "HW")
kr <- bdhs_merge(kr, hw)
kr <- bdhs_harmonize(kr, vars = c("haz_who", "stunted_who"))
```

## Merging recodes

`bdhs_merge()` knows the DHS linking keys, so you don't have to remember them:

| x | y | Keys |
|---|---|---|
| IR, KR, BR | HR | `v001`, `v002` = `hv001`, `hv002` |
| IR | PR | `v001`, `v002`, `v003` = `hv001`, `hv002`, `hvidx` |
| KR, BR | IR | `caseid` |
| KR | PR | `v001`, `v002`, `b16` = `hv001`, `hv002`, `hvidx` |
| PR | HR | `hhid` |
| MR | HR, PR | `mv001`, `mv002` (and `mv003` = `hvidx`) |

```{r}
ir <- bdhs_simulate(2022, "IR")
hr <- bdhs_simulate(2022, "HR")
m <- bdhs_merge(ir, hr)
m[1:3, c("caseid", "v001", "v002", "hv201", "hv205", "hv270")]
```

## Special codes

DHS files use codes like 98 (don't know), 99 (missing) and 9996-9999
(flagged anthropometry), and recent files also use Stata's tagged missing
values. `bdhs_na()` turns them into `NA` using the value labels:

```{r}
x <- haven::labelled(c(1, 2, 8, 9), c(yes = 1, no = 2, "don't know" = 8, missing = 9))
bdhs_na(x)
bdhs_na(x, dont_know = "keep")
```

`bdhs_harmonize()` already does this for every harmonized variable.

## Caveats

* No 1996-97 file was available while the crosswalk was built. Its rules were
  derived from the published codebook and are flagged as unverified in
  `bdhs_harmonized_vars(1997)`.
* District-based variables (`district_bbs`, `division_backcast8`) need a
  district variable, which most rounds do not include.
* Men's files (MR, last collected in 2011) are not yet covered by the
  crosswalk.
